title: Norwegian place, direction, and location words
goal: Choose Norwegian location and direction words, and distinguish where-questions from there-statements.

objectives.statement: Choose Norwegian location and direction words, and distinguish where-questions from there-statements.

These small words tell us whether someone or something is already in a place or is moving toward it.
A location adverb describes where someone or something is:
A directional adverb describes movement toward a place or a change of location:
English often uses the same word in both situations. Norwegian frequently changes the form.

items.value: Use the location form when the action or situation remains in a place.
Use the directional form when someone or something moves toward that place or changes location.

prompt.value: Choose the conversation that makes both people's points of view clear.

options.text: Aisha: Jeg venter der ved biblioteket. Kom dit! Per: Du venter her borte. Jeg går hit nå.
options.why: The forms for Aisha's position, her invitation, and Per's destination do not match the speakers' viewpoints.

options.text: Aisha: Jeg venter her ved biblioteket. Kom hit! Per: Du venter der borte. Jeg går dit nå.
options.why: Aisha locates herself where she is and directs Per toward her; Per locates her away from himself and names her place as his destination.

options.text: Aisha: Jeg venter her ved biblioteket. Kom dit! Per: Du venter der borte. Jeg går hit nå.
options.why: Aisha is inviting Per toward her, and Per is going away from his current location toward Aisha; the directional forms are reversed.

prompt.value: A classmate asks where Emil was and where he went next. Write a message in the correct order: Emil was in room 204, went down to the café by the entrance, and then went home. Also say that the café is one floor below the room. Use location and direction adverbs.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate route-facts, route-order, message-purpose, and place-direction-observation as gating criteria. The response must report positions with location forms and movement with directional forms. Anchors: PASS — «Emil var i rom 204. Så gikk han ned til kafeen, som var nede ved inngangen. Etterpå gikk han hjem.» FAIL route-facts — «Emil var ved kafeen og gikk tilbake til rom 204.» PASS — «Emil var i rom 204. Så gikk han ned til kafeen. Kafeen var nede ved inngangen. Etterpå gikk han hjem.»

criteria.instruction: The message states that Emil was in room 204, went down to the café, states that the café was downstairs by the entrance, and later went home.
The events appear in the order supplied in the task.
The response is a Norwegian message to the classmate about Emil's route.
The message must use location forms for positions and directional forms for movement; failure on this criterion fails the response.

prompt.value: Ida is outside a music school. Per is in the practice room on the second floor. Ida asks which entrance to use and which floor he is on. She goes in and upstairs to him. Later, they go downstairs, out of the building, and to the bus stop. Write the message exchange. Use location adverbs for places and direction adverbs for movement, and keep track of who is speaking.

payload.judge_prompt: Evaluate whether the exchange asks for the entrance and floor, communicates Ida’s route inside and upstairs, and confirms their later trip to the bus stop. Check natural location-versus-direction forms and speaker viewpoint; accept coherent Bokmål wording without requiring fixed expressions.

criteria.instruction: The exchange includes Ida asking Per which entrance to use and which floor he is on.
The exchange communicates that Ida enters the building and reaches Per on the second floor.
The exchange communicates that they later leave the building and head to the bus stop.
The response is a Norwegian text-message exchange that helps Ida arrive and confirms the later plan.
Report whether location forms describe positions and directional forms describe movement; incorrect forms fail the response.
Report whether any her/hit and der/dit forms are consistent with each speaker's viewpoint; inconsistent forms fail the response.
